fields.meta_title: Pricing Page: Examples and How to Build One | Emergent
fields.meta_description: A pricing page shows what each plan costs and what it includes. See four working examples by pricing model and build yours from a prompt.
fields.h1: Build a Pricing Page Where the Numbers Add Up
fields.hero_description: Create a pricing page with a billing switch that does the yearly math and a record of which plan each visitor picks.
fields.features_heading: What Sits Behind the Plan Cards
fields.features_subheading: Plan cards are the visible part. Behind them sit the billing math and a record of every plan visitors choose.
fields.feature_1:
One card per plan, priced as you sell it

List each tier with its price, its billing unit and its top features. Emergent lays out a card per plan, marks the one you recommend and keeps every card the same height.
fields.feature_2:
Monthly and annual prices that agree

A billing switch recalculates every card from one rule you state, such as two months free on yearly plans. Monthly figures and yearly totals both come from that one rule.
fields.feature_3:
A comparison grid that stays readable

Long feature lists move into a grid under the cards, grouped by topic, with plan names pinned to the top as visitors scroll. On a phone the grid shows one plan at a time.
fields.feature_4:
Plan clicks saved to your database

Every press of a plan button lands as a row in a database you own, with the plan and the billing period. Send the rows on to your CRM over its API, or count them by week.
fields.feature_5:
Price changes made by message

Raise a price by sending a message, such as move Team to $32 on March 1. Emergent edits every card and the comparison grid in one change, leaving no stale number on the page.
fields.feature_6:
Code you can take with you

The pricing page and its click table export to GitHub on paid plans. Host both on Emergent with a custom domain, which uses credits, or deploy them beside your sign-up flow.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Pricing Models, Four Working Pages
fields.tab_content_1:
Thirty dollars per seat, twenty-five when billed yearly

Fernway prices its tiers per user and recommends Team. The switch on the page opens on annual billing, where Team reads $25 per user a month, billed as $300 a year, against $30 on monthly billing. The Team card states the yearly saving of $60 per user. Every plan click is saved with the billing period chosen.
fields.tab_content_2:
Send volume in, monthly bill out

Per-email pricing is hard to picture until you see a bill. Relaybird's pricing page takes a monthly send count and prices it: the first 3,000 emails are free, and each 1,000 after that costs $1.00. A developer who types 40,000 sees $37.00 a month. Above 250,000 emails, the calculator gives way to a sales form.
fields.tab_content_3:
Two set packages, with quotes for everything else

Some work has no list price. Halden Studio shows a Brand Sprint at $4,500 and a Website build at $12,000, with a Custom card beside them. Custom opens a short quote form asking for a budget and a launch window. Each request is saved as a row and posted to the studio's #new-business channel in Slack.
fields.tab_content_4:
Which class option is cheapest for how often you come

At Ridgeline Yoga, new students rarely know which option suits them. The pricing page lists a $25 drop-in, a 10-class pack for $200 and Unlimited at $140 a month, then asks how many classes a month each visitor plans. Anyone who answers 8 or more sees that Unlimited costs less than the pack.

fields.howto_title: How to Build a Pricing Page
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to a pricing page that shows each visitor which tier fits and what it will cost.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Settle the model before the layout
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Name each plan for who buys it
fields.howto_step_1_des: Decide what you charge for: seats, usage, a fixed package, or a membership. The model sets the page's shape. Seat pricing wants plan cards, usage wants a calculator, and project work wants a quote form beside a few fixed prices.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Three or four plans fit side by side on a laptop screen. Past that, visitors start comparing columns instead of choosing one. Fold rare needs into a Contact sales card instead of a fifth tier with its own price.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Plan names such as Team or Business tell a visitor where they belong before they read a price. Under each name, write one line on who the plan suits, such as teams of up to 10 people.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Give the plan most customers should pick a label and a stronger border. Visitors who cannot decide take the default. Choose the plan that fits most of your buyers, which is rarely the most expensive one.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Show the annual math in full
fields.howto_step_5_des: If yearly billing is cheaper, print the monthly equivalent, the yearly total and the saving on each card. A discount stated only as a percentage leaves visitors working out the real number for themselves, and many will not bother.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Answer billing questions on the page
fields.howto_step_6_des: Put the questions your sales team hears most under the grid, such as what happens at the seat limit and whether a plan can change mid-cycle. Every question settled on the page is one fewer email before a purchase.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Record every plan button click with the billing period chosen. If nearly everyone picks monthly, the annual saving may be too small to notice. Change one thing at a time and compare a few weeks of clicks.

plan.angle: The top 10 is inspiration: Dribbble and Pinterest boards, pricingpages.design and saaslandingpage.com galleries, a Reddit thread, and example roundups from HubSpot, Mailchimp and Shopify. They show screenshots of pricing pages but never the working parts behind them: the annual toggle and its math, a usage calculator that has to add up, a quote form for work with no fixed price, and a record of which plan buttons people press. This page defines the term up top for the AI Overview, answers the 5 C's question, and shows four working pricing pages by business model, each with the numbers on the page checked.
tab_stories: Fernway sells a project tool in three per-user tiers, and its annual toggle drops the Team plan from $30 to $25 per user a month, billed as $300 a year.
Relaybird prices an email API by volume, so its calculator takes a monthly send count and shows that 40,000 emails cost $37.00 after the first 3,000 free.
Halden Studio lists two fixed design packages and a Custom option whose quote form asks for budget and launch date, then posts each request to the studio's Slack channel.
Ridgeline Yoga sells drop-ins, a 10-class pack and an unlimited month, and asks visitors how often they come so anyone planning 8 or more classes sees that Unlimited costs less.

chip_prompts: Add a billing switch to my three-plan pricing page that opens on annual. Give yearly plans two months free and print the saving on every card.
Below my three plan cards, add a feature grid grouped by topic, with plan names that stay at the top while visitors scroll down the list.
My product charges by usage. Build a pricing page where visitors type their expected monthly volume and see what each plan would cost them.
Add a Custom card next to my three plans that opens a quote form asking for team size, budget, and start date, and save each request to a table.

scope.evidence: H1 'Build a Pricing Page Where the Numbers Add Up', meta title 'Pricing Page: Examples and How to Build One' and hero 'Emergent builds the pricing page with its billing switch, plus a table that records which plan each visitor picks' cover the whole page, not one feature or a sibling topic.

intent.evidence: Top 10 is example galleries and roundups; the page gives four worked examples by pricing model (per-seat, usage calculator, agency packages, class memberships), a definition in FAQ 1, a 7-step how-to and FAQ items on examples, templates, mobile and UI. Meta promise 'four working examples by pricing model' is delivered.

specificity.evidence: Speaks in pricing vocabulary: 'billing unit', 'billing switch', 'two months free on yearly plans', 'Contact sales card', 'seat limit'; comparison table generated from the LP library (Unbounce, Wix, Landingi) with no hub-default fallback.

openers.evidence: Feature bodies open on verbs or full sentences ('List each tier with its price', 'A billing switch recalculates every card', 'Raise a price by sending a message'); tabs open with full sentences ('Fernway prices its tiers per user', 'Some work has no list price'). Two FAQ fragments recorded as notes.

craft.evidence: No tacked-on endings or run-on lists; sentences carry one idea ('Above 250,000 emails, the calculator gives way to a sales form.'). QC Q2/Q5/Q7 clean.

voice.evidence: Concrete, operator voice: 'move Team to $32 on March 1', 'Every question settled on the page is one fewer email before a purchase.' The cross-page 'X hand you Y' why_description formula is a note.

truth.evidence: Math checks: $30 x 12 = $360 vs $300 yearly = $60 saving (two months free); (40,000 - 3,000)/1,000 x $1.00 = $37.00; 8 classes: pack $160 vs Unlimited $140. Emergent claims map to claims_used (free-start 'the free tier covers building and publishing a page', custom-domain 'which uses credits', code-export 'export to GitHub on paid plans'). Table from library (QC V2/V3 pass). Generalizations about unnamed page builders recorded as notes.

distinct.evidence: Four pricing-model tabs (Fernway, Relaybird, Halden Studio, Ridgeline Yoga) unique to this page; no sibling primary (thank you page, one page website) used as a heading; those appear only as FAQ link anchors. QC D2 clean.

faq.evidence: 10 on-topic questions ('What is a pricing page?', 'How to make a pricing page?', 'What is the best design for pricing pages?', 'Where can I find pricing page examples?'...), each answered in its first sentence; hub link in item 2; sibling links 'thank you page' and 'one page website' with exact anchors.

images.evidence: Contact sheet matches copy: tab 1 '$30 per user / $25 per user / $300 per user / Saves $60 per user a year', 'Click saved: Team plan, annual billing'; tab 2 '40,000' -> '$37.00', 'Over 250,000 a month? Talk to sales'; tab 3 '#new-business', 'Brand Sprint $4,500 and Website $12,000'; tab 4 '$140' vs '$160' at 8 classes. One hero each, text readable.

findings.issue: Soft quantifiers about no named third party (every instance listed).
findings.fix: State the specific case or drop the quantifier, e.g. 'Pricing pages often add a feature grid' -> 'A feature grid under the cards answers the detail questions'.

findings.quote: Page builders hand you a pricing table block to fill in.
findings.issue: Unquantified generalization about the competitor category in the table (Unbounce, Wix, Landingi); broadly true and treated as positioning, not a sourced fact.
findings.fix: Tie the contrast to a table row, e.g. code ownership: 'Hosted builders keep the page on their servers. Emergent builds the whole page from one prompt and the code is yours.'

findings.fix: Open the why_description on something this page alone can say, e.g. the annual math or the click table.
